slides.title: Worked example: which design gives better value?
slides.html:
Fictional workshop records: A lifts 31 clips for 9.60; B lifts 42 for 12.00; C lifts 40 for 10.40. These invented records teach the calculation and are not outputs to copy into the assigned simulation.

Use A as this example’s baseline. Find the best value and its percentage improvement over A.
slides.alt: Fictional designs A, B, and C have different clip counts and costs. The strongest lift and best value may belong to different designs.

slides.title: Calculate the baseline value
slides.html: Divide A’s clips by its displayed cost. Record 3.23 clips per cost unit, but retain the full quotient in your calculator for the percentage calculation.
slides.alt: Design A links 31 lifted clips to a displayed build cost of 9.60. Keep the original pair of values.

slides.title: Calculate and compare the other values
slides.html: Calculate each design using its own displayed cost. C has the highest value even though B lifts two more clips. Keep C’s full quotient for the next step.
slides.alt: Two bar comparisons show that B has more clips but C has more clips per cost unit.

slides.title: Substitute the unrounded ratios
slides.html: Compare the new ratio with the baseline ratio, not the two clip counts. Enter the original fractions directly so rounding does not accumulate.
slides.alt: A comparison pathway carries the original C record and the original A baseline into the percentage comparison without rounding intermediate values.

slides.title: Round once and interpret the result
slides.html:
The value increased by 19.1%. This describes clips per cost unit, not energy efficiency or just the change in clip count.

If you use the rounded values 3.85 and 3.23 too early, you get 19.2%. Avoid that error by retaining the original fractions.
slides.alt: A highlighted final answer is contrasted with an early-rounding warning. Round only the final percentage.

slides.title: Apply the method to your own checked designs
slides.html:
Keep one complete record per design. Report each ratio to two decimals, compare at least three distinct designs, and calculate your best design’s percentage improvement over your actual Trial 1 baseline.

For the assigned lab, continue until your best checked ratio rounds to 6.38 within the wire and cost limits. This example’s best ratio of 3.85 is only a practice result.
slides.alt: A design comparison record connects settings, measured outputs, value, and a conclusion supported by the three checked designs.
